# Feature matrix

One-page reference: what runs where. For the readable tour of everything DataQ offers see
[Features](../guides/features.md); for the concepts behind the columns see [Concepts](../get-started/concepts.md) and
[Datasources & checks](../guides/datasources-checks.md).

## Check kinds × datasources

| Check kind | Snowflake | Unity Catalog | PostgreSQLᵖ | ADLS Gen2 (files) | S3 (files)ˢ | Iceberg |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| GX expectations (column / table shape) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Snowflake DMF (native metric functions)ᵈ | ✅ | — | — | — | — | — |
| Custom SQL (rows returned = failures)ᶜ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — | — | — |
| Freshness monitor (hours since latest timestamp) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Freshness from **file arrival time** (no column — catches "no new file") | — | — | — | ✅ | ✅ | — |
| Volume monitor (row count in range) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Anomaly monitor (z-score vs a learned baseline)ᵃ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | — | — | — |
| Schema-drift monitor (column add/drop/type-change vs a stored baseline)ᵇ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Comparison / reconciliation (diff vs a baseline connection) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Column profiler (nulls, distinct, min/max, top values) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Browse for the run target (catalog → schema → table / folders → file) | — | ✅ | ✅ (schema → table) | ✅ | ✅ | — |
| DQ dimension on checks + asset scorecard (coverage + score) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Dry-run preview | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

ᵃ **Live-verified.** The anomaly monitor learns a rolling mean/stddev of the
target's own row count or freshness age (optionally per weekday) and bands each
run's z-score through the usual warn/fail/critical thresholds; below its
`min_points` of history it reports `skip`, never a fabricated pass. Both target
metrics were run against live Snowflake and live Unity Catalog tables via the real
`measure_metric` path — a tick here is earned by an **executed** run against a live
datasource, never by a passing unit test. The dashes are a real restriction, not an omission: the
anomaly executor takes its own measurement over a live SQL connection, while
Iceberg and flat files compute their monitor scalars natively inside their
runners, which stateful kinds never reach.

ᵇ **Schema drift** (ADR 0012)
diffs a live column-name/type snapshot against a stored baseline and flags
add/drop/type-change. Unlike custom SQL it never goes through a `CheckRunner`/GX at
all, so it isn't gated to SQL datasources: introspection is per-datasource —
`information_schema` for Snowflake/Unity Catalog, the Parquet footer or a bounded
CSV header sample for ADLS/S3 flat files, and the loaded table's own metadata for
Iceberg (no data scan on any of them except the CSV sample). Re-baseline explicitly
once a drift is expected and reviewed.

ᶜ **Unity Catalog custom SQL is supported since v1.1.** It runs against a GX
Databricks-SQL batch over the target table. Since v1.2, ordinary catalog
expectations run on that same SQL batch by default — the warehouse evaluates and the
worker never materialises the table; the DataFrame batch remains for
`expect_column_values_to_be_of_type`, suites with a declared sample, and the
`UC_SQL_PUSHDOWN=false` rollback. Verified against a live
Unity Catalog table, including the operational-`error` path when a column will not
resolve. Custom SQL stays binary pass/fail on both SQL datasources (ADR 0019 §4 — a
row count is not a bandable metric), so `metric_value` is null by design, not by
omission.

ᵈ **Snowflake DMF** (ADR [0036](../adr/0036-connection-anchored-check-engines.md)) is the
first platform-native check engine — an alternative `check.engine` for six expectation
types (null count, null percent, duplicate count, unique count, blank count, future-timestamp
percent) plus the freshness monitor, invoking Snowflake's
own `SNOWFLAKE.CORE.*` metric functions instead of a GX expectation. Engine is selected per
check, on a Snowflake connection only; `kind` stays `expectation` either way. Testing or
re-authenticating a Snowflake connection also probes DMF availability (Enterprise Edition +
grant) and stores the result on the connection — surfaced on the connection list and, as a caveat
rather than a hard gate, in the check editor's engine picker. The probe reads zero rows of one
table the connection's role can already see; if the role can see none, or the probe fails for a
reason unrelated to DMFs, the connection shows "couldn't determine" rather than "unavailable".

ᵖ **PostgreSQL** — any server, self-hosted or managed; everything runs by pushdown
on read-only sessions. Every row was verified by an **executed** run against a real
PostgreSQL 16 through the connection's own least-privileged role, and the suite's CI
re-runs that battery (every SQL-capable expectation type, custom SQL, freshness over
`timestamptz`/`timestamp`/`date`, volume, anomaly measurement, profiler, schema drift,
comparison reads,
inventory enumeration and browsing) against the test database on every change. The
profiler reports min/max as unavailable for types PostgreSQL cannot order (`boolean`,
`jsonb`, …) — see [Datasources & checks](../guides/datasources-checks.md#postgresql).

ˢ **S3 means AWS S3 *and* any S3-compatible store** — MinIO, Ceph/RadosGW, Cloudflare R2,
Wasabi, Backblaze B2, SeaweedFS or an on-prem gateway. Set the connection's optional
endpoint URL; every row in this column applies identically either way. See
[Datasources & checks](../guides/datasources-checks.md#s3-compatible-object-stores).

Custom SQL runs a SQL query, so it's **SQL-datasource only** (Snowflake, Unity Catalog, PostgreSQL;
there is no flat-file support, and no issue currently tracks adding it — flat files get freshness/volume monitors instead (see the rows above);
Iceberg is not SQL-queryable — reads go through `pyiceberg` scans, not a query engine).
**Comparison checks** (ADR [0015](../adr/0015-two-connection-comparison-check-model.md))
diff the suite's dataset (the **target under test**) against a baseline on any other
datasource connection — cross-type and cross-env both supported — joined on key columns,
producing matched / mismatched / additional-per-side buckets with a mismatch-% metric,
capped fail-fast reads (`COMPARISON_MAX_ROWS`), redacted samples, and an on-demand
CSV/XLSX report download (derived, never stored). Either SQL side may use a read-only
query projection.

The freshness/volume monitors run on **every datasource** — the SQL datasources, Apache
Iceberg (computed natively via `pyiceberg` scans, not SQL; ADR 0012/0030), and ADLS Gen2 /

- **To your datasources:** each connection type's own transport. A **SQL Server** connection
  (SQL Server, Azure SQL, Synapse, Fabric) is **always** encrypted and **always** verifies the
  server certificate and its hostname — there is no setting that turns either off. The shipped
  driver's own hostname check is broken on current pyOpenSSL, so DataQ replaces it with its own
  (DNS subject-alternative names, a wildcard only as one whole left-most label, an IP only
  against an IP entry, never the certificate's CN) — live-verified to refuse a connection made
  by IP address and one whose certificate chains to an untrusted CA. A PostgreSQL connection
  defaults to `require`; see [Datasources & checks](../guides/datasources-checks.md).
- **Datasource writes:** PostgreSQL sessions are read-only at the server. **SQL Server has no
  equivalent session setting**, so there the protection is the custom-SQL validator plus the
  login's grants: give DataQ a `db_datareader`-only login, as the datasource guide shows.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate docs/site/reference/check-types.md from the code that defines the check types.

Sources (never hand-typed, so the page cannot drift from the product):
  * frontend/src/components/checks/expectationCatalog.ts — what the editor offers

    frontend/scripts/dump-catalog.mts (Vite SSR build; extensionless TS imports need a bundler)
  * backend/app/datasources/expectation_allowlist.py — what the backend will author
    (allowlist-only types, dataframe-only, unbandable), parsed textually so this runs
    without the backend environment
  * backend/app/datasources/unity_catalog.py — SQL_PUSHDOWN_EXPECTATION_TYPES

Usage: scripts/docs/gen-check-catalog.py [--check]   (--check: exit 1 if the page is stale)

input.content:
Found while adding the SQL Server adapter (#1679), which needed T-SQL `[bracket]` identifiers in the ADR 0019 custom-SQL gate (`services/custom_sql.py`).

The gate's `_strip_noncode` only understood `'…'` / `"…"` quotes and comments. Two consequences on engines already in production:

1. **Databricks / Unity Catalog backtick identifiers.** `` SELECT `a'`, 1 FROM {batch}; DELETE FROM t --' `` — the lexer reads `'`, 1 FROM …; DELETE FROM t --'` as ONE string literal and strips it, so it sees a single SELECT. Databricks reads `` `a'` `` as a column name and then a second statement. UC sessions have no server-side read-only guard, so the least-privileged credential is the only remaining protection.
2. **Nested block comments.** PostgreSQL (and SQL Server) nest `/* … */`; the lexer ends a comment at the first `*/`. `SELECT 1 FROM {batch} /* /* */ ' */ ; DELETE FROM t; SELECT '` — the lexer sees a string literal hiding the DELETE, the server sees a comment followed by the DELETE. PostgreSQL sessions are read-only at the server (ADR 0045), so this was defence-in-depth rather than an open write path there; on SQL Server (no session read-only) it would be.

**Fix (in the #1679 PR):** lex each connection type's own delimited-identifier quotes (a query of unknown dialect must pass every lexing), fail closed on a nested block comment (engines disagree on where it ends), and add T-SQL-only forbidden keywords (`OPENQUERY`/`OPENROWSET`/`OPENDATASOURCE`, `BULK`, `DBCC`, `WAITFOR`, `BACKUP`/`RESTORE`, …). Callers now pass the connection type (check authoring, comparison queries, the LLM SQL generator's output gate).

Not verified against a live Databricks warehouse whether (1) is actually exploitable end to end (GX wraps the query; a syntax error would abort the batch) — the fix is correct lexing regardless.

\`backend/tests/services/test_membership_service.py::test_removing_an_env_listed_row_names_the_variable_instead_of_404ing\` then fails:

assert 'OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS' in 'this address is admitted by the environment, not by the members table — remove it from WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS and restart'

With \`WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS\` / \`DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL\` unset the module passes (42/42). So the test reads process env the settings object picks up instead of pinning it, and a developer running the documented local script gets a red suite unrelated to their change. CI is green only because its env does not carry the variable.

Fix: have the test (or an autouse fixture) \`monkeypatch.delenv\` the allowlist variables / override the settings it depends on, so the outcome does not depend on the runner's shell."

content.content:
# ADR 0045 — Engine-generic SQL datasource base

- **Status:** Accepted (2026-09-27)
- **Date:** 2026-09-27
- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
- **Related:** ADR [0010](0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md) / [0013](0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md) (named for the engine, never a hosting vendor), [0019](0019-custom-sql-check-kind.md) (custom SQL), [0036](0036-connection-anchored-check-engines.md) (engines are connection capabilities — these offer GX only), [0040](0040-warehouse-inventory-sync-table-enumeration-seam.md) (table enumeration).

## Context

Theme 8 queues several SQL datasources that GX reaches through a SQLAlchemy dialect and DataQ
reaches with host / port / database / user + password: PostgreSQL first, then MySQL/MariaDB,
then Trino. Snowflake and Unity Catalog each got a hand-written adapter, runner and a set of
entries scattered across the capability sets (custom SQL, monitors, pushdown admission,
profiling, schema drift, inventory, browsing, asset identity). Copying that shape per engine
would make "add a datasource" a dozen-file edit every time — and one missed set is a feature
that silently doesn't work on the new engine.

## Decision

1. **One generic base** (`datasources/generic_sql.py`): a config model, a `ConnectionAdapter`,
   a `CheckRunner` and the catalog helpers, parameterized by a **`SqlEngineSpec`** — the only
   thing an engine supplies: its config subclass (TLS vocabulary, default port, identifier
   limit), driver name, GX datasource factory, `connect_args`, OpenLineage namespace scheme,
   whether the asset name carries the database, its catalog queries, and optional hooks
   (per-column aggregate capability for the profiler, run-path engine options).
2. **One registry** (`datasources/sql_engines.py`). Every capability set that names SQL
   datasources derives from `GENERIC_SQL_TYPES` instead of restating it. Adding an engine is
   one spec module plus one registry entry, a migration widening the connection-type CHECK,
   and the frontend form spec.
3. **Pushdown only.** Expectations run on one GX SQL batch, monitors as scalar Core
   aggregates; nothing is materialised in the worker, so the run target takes no sampling
   block and run admission treats the type as pushdown.
4. **Read only at the session.** Every session DataQ opens is read-only at the server
   (PostgreSQL `default_transaction_read_only`), so a side effect that slips past the ADR 0019
   validator still cannot write.
5. **Names are resolved exactly as spelled**, by the rule `sql.folding_identifier` already
   applies: an all-lower-case name is sent bare, anything else quoted. GX lower-cases an
   unquoted schema, so the GX session is **scoped to the target's schema** (a PostgreSQL
   `search_path`, re-validated through the identifier allowlist before it reaches the session)
   and GX gets no schema at all. Asset identity keeps parts verbatim, so a suite target and an
   enumerated table join byte-for-byte.
6. **Identifier limits are enforced at save time.** PostgreSQL silently truncates a name past
   63 characters, which would resolve a different object; the target resolver refuses it.
7. **Honest gaps, not silent ones.** No column-tag source (classification falls back to the
   suite policy and DataQ's own checks). No warehouse-native lineage: the engines get the
   ADR 0040 *enumeration* half through a separate `TableEnumerator` seam and stay out of
   `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_CONNECTION_TYPES`, so an empty lineage graph reads "not observed".
   Native engines: GX only.

## Consequences

- Every behaviour is verified against a **real server through the real driver** — for a
  value that crosses a driver boundary, only a live run is evidence: the
  PostgreSQL battery dogfoods the test suite's own database, as a least-privileged role, in
  CI. Two driver-boundary defects were found that way on the first run and are now hooks on
  the spec rather than special cases: `min(jsonb)`/`min(boolean)` do not exist (per-column
  profiler capability), and psycopg2's decoded JSON cells crash GX's result formatting
  (JSON kept as text on the run path).
- A new engine inherits the whole feature surface at once — which is the risk as well as the
  point: it is not "supported" until the same battery has run against it.
- Snowflake and Unity Catalog keep their own adapters; they are not migrated onto the base
  (their auth, catalogs and lineage differ too much to gain from it).

input.command:
cat >> docs/site/adr/0045-engine-generic-sql-datasource-base.md <<'EOF'

## Amendment — SQL Server (2026-09-27)

The SQL Server / T-SQL engine ([ADR 0044](0044-mssql-tds-driver-and-entra-auth.md)) is the
first engine that breaks three of the assumptions above, and each became an optional spec hook
rather than a special case:

- **§4 does not hold for it.** TDS has no session-level read-only setting, so a SQL Server
  session is *not* read-only at the server. The guard there is the ADR 0019 validator — now
  lexing each engine's own delimited identifiers (`[…]`, `` `…` ``) — plus a `db_datareader`
  login, which the docs require. The base's promise is restated per engine, not assumed.
- **§5's session scoping does not exist.** A login's default schema is fixed on the server, so
  `session_schema = False` hands GX the schema instead; SQL Server's usual case-insensitive
  collations resolve it whatever GX's casing (a mixed-case schema on a case-sensitive
  collation is a documented limitation).
- **One secret can be two kinds of credential.** An Entra service principal's client secret
  goes to a token endpoint, not the server, so the spec owns its URL and connect args (a
  subclass overriding `url` / `engine_args`), declares its own `destination_fields`, and names
  its secret (`credential_noun`).

Two more hooks came with it: `explain_failure`, which turns a failure the engine *knows* (a
documented driver limitation, a missing optional driver) into a DataQ-authored message shown
verbatim; and `unsupported_expectation_types`, for an allowlisted type the dialect has no GX
translation for (regex on T-SQL), refused at author time rather than erroring on every run.
EOF

def __init__(self, spec: SqlEngineSpec) -> None:
        self.spec = spec

    # #1401: the host and port decide which server receives the password.
    destination_fields: ClassVar[dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]] = {"secret": ("host", "port")}

    def validate_config(self, raw: dict[str, Any]) -> GenericSqlConfig:
        return self.spec.validate_config(raw)

    def test(self, raw: dict[str, Any], secret: str | None, **_: Any) -> None:
        """Open a session and run ``SELECT 1``; raise on any failure."""
        if secret is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"a password is required to test a {self.spec.display_name} connection"
            )
        from sqlalchemy import text

        engine = self.spec.create_engine(self.validate_config(raw), secret)
        try:
            with engine.connect() as conn:
                conn.execute(text("SELECT 1"))
        finally:
            engine.dispose()


class GenericSqlCheckRunner:
    """`CheckRunner` for a generic SQL engine: one GX SQL batch per run, monitors by scalar SQL."""

    # Runner-advertised monitor capability (#429): EXPLICITLY what this runner implements.
    supported_monitor_kinds: ClassVar[frozenset[str]] = frozenset({FRESHNESS, VOLUME})
    # The run path hands a `value_signal_gate` only to runners advertising it (#2014).
    accepts_value_signal_gate: ClassVar[bool] = True

    def __init__(self, spec: SqlEngineSpec, config: GenericSqlConfig, secret: str) -> None:
        self._spec = spec
        self._config = config
        self._secret = secret
        # The runner's ONE lazily-built engine (#427) for the non-GX SQL (monitors).
        self._engine = LazyEngine(self._build_engine)

    def _build_engine(self) -> Any:
        # pool_pre_ping: the session can sit idle across a long GX validation.
        return self._spec.create_engine(
            self._config,
            self._secret,
            timeout=None,
            pool_pre_ping=True,
            **self._spec.run_engine_options,
        )

    def close(self) -> None:
        """Dispose the shared engine's pool. Idempotent; a no-op if never used."""
        self._engine.close()

    def run_checks(
        self,
        *,
        table: str,
        schema: str | None,
        checks: list[CheckSpec],
        index_columns: list[str] | None = None,
        value_signal_gate: ValueSignalGate | None = None,
    ) -> SuiteOutcome:
        temp_types = self._spec.temp_table_types
        writable = [i for i, spec in enumerate(checks) if spec.expectation_type in temp_types]
        if not writable:
            return self._run_batch(
                table=table,
                schema=schema,
                checks=checks,
                index_columns=index_columns,
                value_signal_gate=value_signal_gate,
                read_only=True,
            )
        guarded = [i for i in range(len(checks)) if i not in set(writable)]
        by_position: dict[int, CheckOutcome] = {}
        success = True
        for positions, read_only in ((guarded, True), (writable, False)):
            if not positions:
                continue
            outcome = self._run_batch(
                table=table,
                schema=schema,
                checks=[checks[i] for i in positions],
                index_columns=index_columns,
                value_signal_gate=value_signal_gate,
                read_only=read_only,
            )
            success = success and outcome.success
            by_position.update(zip(positions, outcome.checks, strict=True))
        return SuiteOutcome(success=success, checks=[by_position[i] for i in range(len(checks))])

    def _run_batch(
        self,
        *,
        table: str,
        schema: str | None,
        checks: list[CheckSpec],
        index_columns: list[str] | None,
        value_signal_gate: ValueSignalGate | None,
        read_only: bool,
    ) -> SuiteOutcome:
        import great_expectations as gx

        from backend.app.datasources.gx_runner import run_expectations

        # GX lower-cases an unquoted schema name, which on an engine that resolves names exactly
        # as spelled retargets a mixed-case schema. So the SESSION is scoped to the target's
        # schema instead (the engine's default schema) and GX gets no schema at all.
        scoped = self._spec.scoped_config(self._config, schema)
        connections = GxConnectionSource(self._spec, scoped, self._secret, read_only=read_only)
        context = gx.get_context(mode="ephemeral")
        datasource: Any = None
        try:
            # GX tests the connection inside `add_*`, so a failure there must still close it.
            datasource = self._spec.gx_datasource(
                context,
                f"{self._spec.conn_type}-{table}",
                self._spec.url_string(scoped, self._secret),
                {
                    "connect_args": self._spec.connect_args(scoped, None, read_only=read_only),
                    "creator": connections.connect,
                    **self._spec.run_engine_options,
                },
            )
            asset = datasource.add_table_asset(
                name=table, table_name=gx_table_name(table), schema_name=None
            )
            batch_definition = asset.add_batch_definition_whole_table(name="whole_table")
            return run_expectations(
                context,
                batch_definition=batch_definition,
                checks=checks,
                name=f"suite-{table}",
                index_columns=index_columns,
                value_signal_gate=value_signal_gate,
            )
        finally:
            if datasource is not None:
                _dispose_gx_engine(datasource)
            connections.close()

    def run_monitors(

"""Print every conflict hunk (ours / theirs) of the given files, or resolve simple ones.

usage: hunks.py show FILE...          print hunks with indices
       hunks.py union FILE IDX...     resolve hunk IDX as theirs-then-ours (both kept)
       hunks.py ours FILE IDX... / theirs FILE IDX...
"""

import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path("/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/worktrees/agent-a3547145db0057401")
PAT = re.compile(r"<<<<<<< [^\n]*\n(.*?)=======\n(.*?)>>>>>>> [^\n]*\n", re.S)


def show(files: list[str]) -> None:
    for f in files:
        text = (ROOT / f).read_text()
        for i, m in enumerate(PAT.finditer(text)):
            print(f"=== {f} #{i}\n--- ours\n{m.group(1)}--- theirs\n{m.group(2)}")


def resolve(mode: str, f: str, idxs: list[int]) -> None:
    path = ROOT / f
    text = path.read_text()
    out, pos = [], 0
    for i, m in enumerate(PAT.finditer(text)):
        out.append(text[pos : m.start()])
        ours, theirs = m.group(1), m.group(2)
        if i in idxs or not idxs:
            out.append(
                {"union": theirs + ours, "unionours": ours + theirs, "ours": ours, "theirs": theirs}[mode]
            )
        else:
            out.append(m.group(0))
        pos = m.end()
    out.append(text[pos:])
    path.write_text("".join(out))


if sys.argv[1] == "show":
    show(sys.argv[2:])
else:
    resolve(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], [int(x) for x in sys.argv[3:]])

=== docs/site/guides/datasources-checks.md #2
--- ours
### SQL Server / Azure SQL / Fabric (T-SQL)

One connection type (`mssql`) for **anything that speaks SQL Server's TDS protocol** — SQL
Server itself, Azure SQL Database, Synapse dedicated pools, and the Microsoft Fabric SQL
endpoints (Warehouse, Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint, SQL database in Fabric). It is named for
the engine, not a cloud (ADR [0010](../adr/0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md)),
and sits on the same generic SQL base as PostgreSQL. The driver decision and its trade-offs are
[ADR 0044](../adr/0044-mssql-tds-driver-and-entra-auth.md). Live-verified against Azure SQL
Database with both auth modes.

- **Fields:** host (a bare hostname — e.g. `myserver.database.windows.net`; no scheme, port or
  `\instance`: connect to a named instance by its port), port (default 1433), database, an
  optional default schema (default `dbo`), and one of two **auth modes**:
    - **SQL login** — `user`, and the password as the secret. SQL Server, Azure SQL, Synapse.
    - **Entra service principal** — `tenant_id` and `client_id`, and the client secret as the
      secret. DataQ asks Entra ID for a token for `https://database.windows.net/` and presents
      it at login; the client secret never goes to the database server. Azure SQL, Synapse and
      Fabric. The principal must exist in the database (`CREATE USER [app-name] FROM EXTERNAL
      PROVIDER`) with read access. DataQ cannot read a client secret's expiry — track it in
      Entra ID and re-authenticate before it lapses. Managed identity and certificate
      credentials are not supported yet.
- **TLS is always on and always verified.** There is no TLS mode to choose: every connection is
  encrypted, the server certificate must chain to a trusted CA (the public roots DataQ ships,
  or a **private CA certificate** you paste into the connection for a self-hosted server), and
  the hostname must match the certificate. Connecting by IP address fails for that reason — use
  the name on the certificate. The shipped driver speaks TLS 1.2; TDS 8 "strict" encryption is
  not supported yet.
- **Read only — by grant, not by session.** Unlike PostgreSQL and MySQL, SQL Server has no
  per-session read-only switch, so DataQ **cannot make the server refuse a write**. The guards
  are the custom-SQL validator (which understands T-SQL `[bracket]` identifiers and refuses
  `OPENQUERY`/`OPENROWSET`/`OPENDATASOURCE`, `BULK`, `DBCC`, `WAITFOR`, `BACKUP`/`RESTORE`
  and the rest of the ADR 0019 list) and **the login you give DataQ, which must be read-only**:

  ```sql
  -- in the target database
  CREATE USER dataq_reader FOR LOGIN dataq_reader;   -- or FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for Entra
  ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER dataq_reader;
  ```

  Nothing else is needed: the session-scoped `#temp` tables some SQL Server queries use need no
  extra grant (verified with a `db_datareader`-only login).
- **Two driver lanes** (`driver`):
    - **`python-tds`** (default) — pure-Python and MIT-licensed, shipped in the DataQ image. It
      covers SQL Server, Azure SQL and Synapse.
    - **`odbc`** — Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 through `pyodbc`. DataQ **does not ship** this
      driver (its licence does not allow us to redistribute it — ADR 0044), so this lane only
      works in an image **you** build on top of DataQ's — a sketch (DataQ's CI does not build
      or test it, since doing so would mean accepting the driver's licence):

      ```dockerfile
      FROM ghcr.io/theurgicduke771/dataq-backend:latest
      USER root
      RUN apt-get update && ACCEPT_EULA=Y apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
            msodbcsql18 unixodbc && pip install pyodbc && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
      USER 10001
      ```

      (add Microsoft's apt repository first, as Microsoft's install guide describes). Pick
      `odbc` on the connection; an optional `odbc_driver` names a different installed driver.
      If the lane is chosen but the driver or `pyodbc` is missing, **Test** says exactly that
      and how to fix it. On this lane the driver's own certificate checking applies (encryption
      required, server certificate verified against the image's trust store).
- **Microsoft Fabric SQL endpoints need the ODBC lane today.** Over the default `python-tds`
  driver, Fabric rejects the login after routing it (a known incompatibility in that driver,
  still being worked on); Test and runs say so and point at the ODBC lane instead of showing the
  raw driver error. Fabric accepts Entra ID only, and
  two things are set up on the Fabric side: the tenant setting **Service principals can use
  Fabric APIs**, and a workspace role (or item permission) for the principal. If Fabric refuses
  the principal's login on the ODBC lane, Test names those two prerequisites.
- **Everything runs in the database**, as on PostgreSQL. A run target takes no sampling block
  (so no `TABLESAMPLE`). Freshness reads `datetimeoffset` as the instant it is (offset
  honoured), `datetime2`/`datetime` as UTC, and `date` as midnight UTC.
- **Regular expressions are not available**: T-SQL has no regex operator Great Expectations can
  translate to, so the four regex expectations are refused when you save them (and hidden in
  the editor). Use a custom-SQL check with `LIKE` or `PATINDEX`. Value-length checks use
  T-SQL `LEN`, which ignores trailing spaces.
- **Type checks** (`to_be_of_type`, `in_type_list`) compare the bare type name: `DECIMAL` for
  `decimal(12,2)`, `INTEGER` for `int`, `NVARCHAR`, `DATETIME2`, `DATETIMEOFFSET`, `BIT`.
- **The profiler** reports min/max as unavailable (null) for types SQL Server has no MIN/MAX for
  — `bit`, `xml`, `geography`/`geometry`, `text`/`ntext`/`image`, `json`, `vector` — and distinct
  count / top values as unavailable for all of those except `bit`.
- **Names** resolve under the database's collation. On the usual case-insensitive collations
  any casing reaches the object; on a **case-sensitive** collation, a mixed-case *schema* in a
  run target is not supported (the check engine lower-cases it), though mixed-case tables and
  columns are.
- **No column tags.** DataQ does not read SQL Server's sensitivity classifications
  (`sys.sensitivity_classifications`) yet — reading them needs a permission a reader login
  usually lacks, and without it the catalog view silently returns nothing, which DataQ would
  otherwise report as "no sensitive columns". Columns are classified by the suite's column
  policy and DataQ's own checks. There is no warehouse-native lineage either.
- **Inventory sync and browsing** list the tables and views in `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` that the
  login can `SELECT`; the fixed-role schemas every database carries (`db_datareader`, …) are
  never offered.
- **Speed.** The shipped driver is pure Python. DataQ pushes aggregates to the server and caps
  samples, so this rarely matters, but every query is one network round trip — a suite run
  from a region far from the database is dominated by latency, not by the database.
- **Azure SQL serverless** databases pause when idle. The first login resumes them, which can
  take up to a minute: a run waits for it, a Test Connection gives up after 10 seconds — test
  again once the database is awake.

||||||| 35b4c987
--- theirs
### MySQL / MariaDB

One connection type for **any MySQL or MariaDB server**, on the same generic SQL base as
PostgreSQL. The driver is **PyMySQL** (MIT); the GPL-licensed MySQL drivers are never used.
Live-verified against MySQL 8.4, MariaDB 11.8 and MariaDB 10.6 (the long-term line many
managed services still default to).

- **Fields:** host, port (default 3306), database, user, and the password as the secret. A
  MySQL *schema* is a database, so a run target's optional schema names another database
  (it defaults to the connection's).
- **TLS:** the same modes as PostgreSQL, `require` by default. `require` encrypts and refuses a
  server without TLS (PyMySQL's own default would quietly fall back to plaintext); `verify-*`
  also checks the certificate against the system trust store, so a server with MySQL's
  self-generated certificate fails them.
- **Read only, UTC.** Every session runs `SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY` (the statement
  every version accepts — the `transaction_read_only` variable does not exist before
  MariaDB 11.1) and sets `time_zone = '+00:00'`, so a
  `TIMESTAMP` column comes back in UTC and freshness is right whatever the server's zone is
  (`DATETIME` has no zone and is read as UTC). **One exception:** GX checks uniqueness on
  MySQL by copying the column into session temporary tables, which a read-only transaction
  refuses — so *Column values unique* runs on its own session without the read-only guard.
  No SQL you wrote ever runs there. It needs the `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLES` grant; without it
  that one check errors and the rest of the suite is unaffected:

  ```sql
  CREATE USER 'dataq_reader'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '…';
  GRANT SELECT, SHOW VIEW, CREATE TEMPORARY TABLES ON shop.* TO 'dataq_reader'@'%';
  ```

- **Collation decides equality.** Uniqueness, set membership and comparisons follow the
  column's collation: under the default case-insensitive one, `'a'` and `'A'` are duplicates.
  Column names are case-insensitive; **table and database names are case-sensitive** on a Linux
  server (`lower_case_table_names=0`), so type them exactly as the server shows them.
- **Types:** `BOOLEAN` is `TINYINT(1)` (values `0`/`1`); MariaDB's `JSON` is `LONGTEXT`, which is
  what schema drift reports for it.
- **No column tags, no warehouse-native lineage** — as for PostgreSQL. Inventory sync and the
  schema browser list what `information_schema` shows the user, which is privilege-filtered.

without the read-only guard and needs the `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLES` grant; and

`'A'` are duplicates under the default case-insensitive one) — see

user-installed ODBC lane) Microsoft Fabric SQL endpoints; SQL login or Entra service princ

"""widen connection type-set for the generic SQL Server / T-SQL datasource (#1679)

Adds ``mssql`` to ``ck_connections_type_valid``. Widening a CHECK is backward compatible: the
running image never writes the new value, so it deploys ahead of (or with) the adapter.

Rollback: downgrade restores the previous set — safe only while no ``mssql`` connection row
exists (the re-added CHECK would fail validation against one). Delete those rows first.
"""

from collections.abc import Sequence

from alembic import op

# revision identifiers, used by Alembic.

_BEFORE = (
    "'snowflake', 'adls_gen2', 's3', 'unity_catalog', 'iceberg', 'postgres', 'mysql', 'adf', "
    "'airflow', 'dbt'"
)
_AFTER = (
    "'snowflake', 'adls_gen2', 's3', 'unity_catalog', 'iceberg', 'postgres', 'mysql', 'mssql', "
    "'adf', 'airflow', 'dbt'"
)


def _set_type_check(values: str) -> None:
    # IF EXISTS on the drop so a partial-retry after an aborted run re-applies cleanly.
    op.execute("ALTER TABLE connections DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS ck_connections_type_valid")

        f"CHECK (type IN ({values}))"
    )


def upgrade() -> None:
    _set_type_check(_AFTER)


def downgrade() -> None:
    _set_type_check(_BEFORE)

content.content:
Skill "code-review" completed (forked execution).

Result:
I found 6 issues in `feature/issue-1679-mssql-adapter` against `origin/main`: 4 medium, 2 low. The ReportFindings tool isn't available in this session, so the full findings are here. I didn't run any tests. Findings 1–3 are backed by the installed GX and pytds source; finding 4 depends on SQL Server behaviour I haven't confirmed.

1. **`backend/app/datasources/generic_sql.py:523` (medium).** On SQL Server the schema is handed to GX without quotes. GX lower-cases any unquoted schema name (`great_expectations/datasource/fluent/sql_datasource.py:1088`).
   - A Fabric Warehouse uses a case-sensitive collation by default (`Latin1_General_100_BIN2_UTF8`), and SQL Server or Azure SQL databases can too.
   - So a target of `Sales.Orders` becomes `sales."Orders"`, and every check against it fails with "invalid object name".
   - Freshness/volume monitors on the same target keep working, because they go through SQLAlchemy Core, which quotes the name.
   - Fix: quote the schema the same way `gx_table_name` quotes the table.

2. **`backend/app/services/failure_classifier.py:283` (medium).** The new `"login failed for user"` marker is meant to exclude error 4060 (the login is valid but can't open the database). That exclusion doesn't hold:
   - SQL Server sends 4060 followed by 18456 on the same login.
   - pytds joins every server message into one exception text (`tds_session.raise_db_exception`), and pyodbc concatenates its error records the same way.
   - The combined text contains "Login failed for user 'x'", so a missing database grant is reported as a dead or expired credential.

3. **`backend/app/services/custom_sql.py:92` (medium).** The T-SQL forbidden-keyword list misses several write and permission statements. This matters more here than on the other engines:
   - T-SQL runs several statements in one batch without any `;` between them.
   - SQL Server connections have no read-only session setting.
   - GX runs the custom query text directly as a batch (`_get_sqlalchemy_records_from_substituted_batch_subquery`).
   - So `SELECT TOP 1 @p = TEXTPTR(c) FROM t WRITETEXT t.c @p 'x'` passes validation. `UPDATETEXT`, `DENY`, `RECEIVE`, `ENABLE`/`DISABLE TRIGGER` and `CHECKPOINT` all get through the same way.
   - The only remaining guard is the least-privileged login the docs ask for.

4. **`backend/app/services/custom_sql.py:127` (medium).** The validator treats a `--` comment as running until `\n` only. PostgreSQL's parser also ends a line comment at a lone `\r`, and SQL Server very likely does too.
   - Given `SELECT 1 FROM t --x\rDELETE FROM t`, the validator strips everything after `--` and never sees the DELETE.
   - The server ends the comment at `\r` and runs the DELETE. On SQL Server there's no `;` requirement or read-only session to stop it.
   - Fix: end a line comment at `\r` as well.

5. **`backend/app/services/dataset_reader.py:114` (low).** For SQL Server, both the `COUNT(*)` query and the new `.subquery()` wrap the user's comparison query as a subquery in the FROM clause. T-SQL rejects such a subquery in two cases that PostgreSQL and MySQL accept:
   - A column with no name, such as `amount*2` (error 8155).
   - A top-level `ORDER BY` without `TOP` (error 1033).
   - A query like `SELECT id, amount*2 FROM orders` passes validation but fails with an unclear error on every run.
   - GX already strips `ORDER BY` for SQL Server in its own query metrics. Doing the same here, or refusing these queries when the check is authored, would close it.

6. **`backend/app/datasources/mssql.py:198` (low).** `_ca_file` writes the private CA bundle to a predictable path in the shared temp directory. If a file already exists there, it's used without checking its contents.
   - On a host where other users can write to `/tmp`, one could create that file first with their own CA. The connection would then accept a man-in-the-middle certificate.
   - Fix: use a private directory (created with `mkdtemp` or owned by the app, mode 0700), or verify the file's contents before reusing it.

Summary:
- `backend/app/datasources/generic_sql.py:523` — GX lower-cases the unquoted schema, so mixed-case schemas break on case-sensitive collations such as Fabric's default.
- `backend/app/services/failure_classifier.py:283` — "login failed for user" also appears in 4060 messages, so a missing database grant is classified as a dead credential.
- `backend/app/services/custom_sql.py:92` — the T-SQL forbidden list misses WRITETEXT, UPDATETEXT, DENY, RECEIVE and DISABLE TRIGGER, and T-SQL runs multiple statements without `;`.
- `backend/app/services/custom_sql.py:127` — `--` comments end only at `\n`, so a lone `\r` can hide a trailing statement from the validator.
- `backend/app/services/dataset_reader.py:114` — SQL Server's subquery rules (unnamed columns, `ORDER BY`) make otherwise valid comparison queries fail at run time.
- `backend/app/datasources/mssql.py:198` — the CA bundle path is predictable and an existing file is trusted as-is, so a planted CA is possible on shared hosts.

def _ca_file(config: MssqlConfig) -> str:
    """The CA bundle python-tds must verify against — never ``None``, which would turn TLS off.

    A private CA is written into a directory this process created (``mkdtemp``: mode 0700, a

SQL Server cannot scope a session to a schema, so the generic SQL runner hands the run target's schema to GX (\`session_schema=False\`). GX 1.17.2 lower-cases an unquoted \`schema_name\` (\`sql_datasource.py\` \`_to_lower_if_not_bracketed_by_quotes\`). Freshness/volume monitors and the profiler are unaffected (SQLAlchemy Core quotes the name).

Why it isn't a one-line fix: passing \`quoted_name(schema, quote=True)\` survives GX's lower-casing, but GX's \`TableAsset.test_connection\` (run inside \`add_table_asset\`) then compares it against the inspector's schema names *after lower-casing those*, so a quoted mixed-case schema is refused on **every** collation. A '\"Sales\"' string is rendered by the dialect as \`[\"Sales\"]\`. Options: a GX query asset (\`SELECT * FROM [Sales].[Orders]\`) for mixed-case schemas on mssql, or bypassing \`test_connection\` via our own asset construction; either needs a live run on a CS-collation database (Fabric via the ODBC lane, or an Azure SQL DB created with a CS collation).

Currently documented as a limitation in the datasources guide (SQL Server section → Names)."

A comparison check's per-side SQL projection is read as a derived table (\`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (<query>) __dataq_src\`, then a Core \`.limit()\` select over the same subquery — \`services/dataset_reader.py\`). T-SQL rejects two shapes inside a derived table that PostgreSQL/MySQL accept:

- a column with no name, e.g. \`SELECT id, amount*2 FROM orders\` (Msg 8155);
- a top-level \`ORDER BY\` without \`TOP\`/\`OFFSET\` (Msg 1033).

Such a query passes the ADR 0019 validator and then fails on every run with a driver error the classifier cannot make useful. Fix: refuse them at author time on \`mssql\` with a message that says what to change (alias the column; drop the ORDER BY — the comparison engine sorts itself), or strip a trailing ORDER BY the way GX does for its own SQL Server metrics. Needs a live check on Azure SQL."

input.content:
## Summary

- **One `mssql` datasource type** for everything that speaks SQL Server's TDS protocol — SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Synapse, and Microsoft Fabric SQL endpoints — as a `SqlEngineSpec` on the generic SQL base (ADR 0045), per the accepted ADR 0044. Auth: `sql` (user + password) or `entra_service_principal` (tenant_id + client_id + client secret → `ClientSecretCredential` token for `https://database.windows.net/.default`, passed as `access_token_callable`; the secret never enters the URL).
- **Default driver `python-tds` + `sqlalchemy-pytds`** (both MIT, from installed metadata), with DataQ's own fixes in `datasources/mssql_tds.py`: a SAN hostname validator via `cryptography` (DNS SANs, single-label wildcard, IP only against IP SANs, no CN fallback, `\instance` stripped) replacing pytds's broken one, and named-instance routing (resolve only the host part). **TLS is always on**: a CA bundle (certifi, or the connection's private CA written into a per-process 0700 dir) is always passed and `validate_host` is always `True`; `sslmode` can only be `verify-full`.
- **Optional ODBC lane** (`driver: odbc` → `mssql+pyodbc`, Encrypt=yes, TrustServerCertificate=no, driver-native Entra). DataQ never adds msodbcsql18/pyodbc to requirements or images; if chosen but absent, Test Connection says exactly that and how to build a derived image. **Fabric on python-tds** (#2126) is reported honestly — the known limitation + the ODBC-lane fix — instead of the raw "system update" login error; on the ODBC lane an Entra login refusal names the Fabric prerequisites.
- **Generic base hooks** (no fork): `session_schema` (SQL Server can't scope a session to a schema → GX gets it), spec-level `destination_fields`, `credential_noun`, `explain_failure` (a DataQ-authored `SafeMonitorError` — the one failure text a connection test now returns to the client), `unsupported_expectation_types` (regex: no T-SQL translation in GX, refused at author time + hidden in the editor), `llm_dialect`. ADR 0045 amended.
- **Custom-SQL gate is now dialect-aware** (a real pre-existing gap, filed as #2134): lexes `[bracket]` / `` `backtick` `` identifiers per connection type (unknown dialect must pass every lexing), rejects nested block comments, ends `--` at a lone CR, and on mssql refuses `OPENQUERY/OPENROWSET/OPENDATASOURCE`, `BULK`, `DBCC`, `WAITFOR`, `BACKUP/RESTORE`, `WRITETEXT/UPDATETEXT`, `DENY`, `ENABLE/DISABLE`, … (T-SQL runs unseparated statements in one batch, and TDS has **no session read-only** — documented: the login must be `db_datareader`).
- Everything else via the shared registries: capability sets, inventory (`INFORMATION_SCHEMA` + `HAS_PERMS_BY_NAME`), browse, profiler column caps (live-verified T-SQL aggregate support), comparison reads (Core `.limit()` → `TOP`), auth markers (18456 with a 4060 veto; Entra secret markers shared with #2130), LLM dialect entry, migration widening the type CHECK (chained after MySQL's `d0cccce55833`), frontend form/targets/labels, docs.

## Linked issue

Fixes #1679. Refs #2126 (Fabric on python-tds). Filed from this work: #2134, #2135, #2137, #2138.

## Type of change

- [x] feat — new functionality
- [x] fix — bug fix (custom-SQL lexer gap, #2134)
- [x] docs

## Checklist

- [x] **Manually tested locally** — live battery below
- [x] **Single functionality** (the custom-SQL lexer fix was required by T-SQL brackets and is its own commit)
- [x] **Conventional commit title**
- [x] **No secrets, credentials, or `.env` files committed**
- [x] **Black + Ruff + mypy pass locally** (mypy incl. tests: 523 files clean)
- [x] **Prettier + ESLint + tsc pass locally**
- [x] **Tests added/updated** — backend 7165 passed / 97.22% cov; frontend 1517 passed / 88.5% lines
- [x] **`/code-review` agent review run** — 6 findings: 4 fixed in-PR (4060 misclassified as dead credential, CR-terminated comment bypass, missing T-SQL write keywords, predictable CA path), 2 filed (#2137 mixed-case schema on CS collation — GX limitation, documented; #2138 T-SQL derived-table rules in comparison queries — documented)
- [x] **Docs / ADRs updated** — datasources guide (SQL Server/Azure SQL/Fabric section, ODBC lane how-to, Fabric limitation), feature matrix (column ᵗ + lineage row), security (TLS always verified; no session read-only; column-tag gap), changelog, check-types (regenerated), openapi/mcp docs (`--check` clean), ADR 0045 amendment, CLAUDE.md
- [x] **`docs/progress.md` — N/A** for this PR (left to the orchestrator's progress PR)
- [x] **Security implications considered** — TLS always verified (validator replaced, negative live cases below), secret never in URL, #1401 destination fields (`host, port, auth_type, tenant_id, client_id, ca_certificate, driver`), validator hardening, no session read-only documented

## Schema migration?

- [x] Yes — `0b451979c77d` widens `ck_connections_type_valid` with `mssql`; `down_revision = d0cccce55833` (main's single head). **Tested up → down → up** on a scratch DB. Rollback: downgrade restores the previous set, safe only while no `mssql` row exists. **If #2132 (Trino, `1a95d7c34808`) merges first, this must be re-chained after it (and its `_BEFORE`/`_AFTER` sets updated).**

## Manual test notes — live evidence (Azure SQL free offer `dataq_test`, `dbo.Orders`, read-only)

Opt-in live lane `backend/tests/integration/test_mssql_live.py` (skipped unless `DATAQ_MSSQL_LIVE_HOST` is set — no SQL Server can run in CI without a commercial licence), run through the **real adapter, CheckRunner, monitors, profiler, browse, inventory and `run_service.execute_run` against a private Postgres app DB**: **17 passed** on the adapter branch head (`1f869f2f` era):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| SQL login (`dataq_reader`, db_datareader) over verified TLS | ✅ connects; wrong password → `is_auth_failure`, PERMISSION |
| Entra service principal (`dataq-terraform-sp`, contained db_datareader) via token | ✅ connects; wrong client secret (AADSTS7000215) → dead credential |
| Connect **by IP** (hostname mismatch) | ✅ refused: `Certificate does not match host name '<ip>'` (CONNECTIVITY) |
| **Untrusted CA** (private CA unrelated to the server) | ✅ refused: `certificate verify failed` |
| **Fabric Warehouse** on python-tds (SP, workspace admin) | ✅ `KnownDatasourceLimitationError` with the limitation + ODBC-lane fix (driver cause: "Couldn't complete the operation due to a system update…") |
| Every SQL-capable expectation type by pushdown, **both auth modes** | ✅ expected verdicts; the 4 regex types **error** on T-SQL → now refused at author time |
| Freshness over `datetimeoffset` (offset honoured: `08:00-07:00` read as 15:00 UTC, `pytds.tz.FixedOffsetTimezone`) / `datetime2` (naive→UTC) / `date`; volume | ✅ both auth modes |
| Anomaly measurement (row_count, freshness_age_hours) | ✅ |
| Profiler (no MIN/MAX over `bit`; Decimal min/max) | ✅ |
| list columns, schema drift, comparison reads (table + T-SQL query) | ✅ |
| Inventory enumeration + browse (only `dbo`; fixed-role schemas never offered) | ✅ |
| Suite run persisted end-to-end (fail/fail/pass/pass incl. Decimal samples in JSONB) | ✅ |
| `#temp` tables with a db_datareader-only login | ✅ no extra grant needed (probe) |
| Driver-boundary types | NUMERIC→`Decimal`, datetime2→naive `datetime`, datetimeoffset→aware `datetime` w/ `pytds.tz.FixedOffsetTimezone`, bit→`bool` (unit tests use these exact types) |

**Honest caveat:** after merging #2125/#2130 into the branch, a re-run of the live lane could not reach the server — the Azure SQL firewall allows only the previous egress IP and this machine's egress is now **103.175.62.210** (firewall rules deliberately not changed). The post-merge changes on the live path (base `create_engine` plumbing, `sslmode` pin, private CA dir, auth veto, lexer) are covered by unit tests and mutation-checked; the live lane should be re-run once the IP is allowed.

**ODBC lane not exercised live** (msodbcsql18 is not installed here and was deliberately not installed system-wide); lane selection, URL/`Encrypt`/`TrustServerCertificate`, Entra `Authentication=ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipal`, and both "driver absent" messages are unit-tested.

**Mutation checks:** 19 mutations of the fixes (wildcard rules, IP/CN fallback, instance stripping, cafile/validate_host, GX schema hand-off, Fabric explanation, secret-in-URL, regex gate, sslmode pin, safe-message pass-through, 18456 marker, 4060 veto, CR comment end, WRITETEXT, bracket lexing, nested comments) — all KILLED by their regression tests.

**Licences:** python-tds 1.17.1 MIT, sqlalchemy-pytds 1.0.2 MIT, pyOpenSSL 26.4.0 Apache-2.0 (now a direct pin), certifi 2026.7.22 MPL-2.0 (unmodified, weak copyleft — OK under rule 40). pip-audit: no known vulnerabilities.

## Security / risk notes

- TDS has no session read-only: a SQL Server connection's write protection is the (hardened) custom-SQL gate + a `db_datareader` login. Stated in the guide, feature matrix and security page.
- Two single-maintainer driver packages, exact-pinned; `mssql_tds.install()` refuses a pytds whose shape it doesn't recognise, so a bump can't silently re-enable the broken validator.
- Column sensitivity classifications (`sys.sensitivity_classifications`) are deliberately **not** read yet: without VIEW permission the view silently returns nothing, which would read as "nothing sensitive" (documented as DataQ's gap).

**Design**
- `datasources/mssql.py` adds one `mssql` engine spec on the shared SQL base, registered alongside Postgres and MySQL. It is a small subclass that overrides only how the URL and connection arguments are built.
- Auth works in two modes:
  - SQL login: user plus password.
  - Entra service principal: tenant and client ID plus a client secret. The token comes from `ClientSecretCredential` for `https://database.windows.net/.default` and is passed as `access_token_callable`. The client secret never goes into the URL.

- `datasources/mssql_tds.py` ships both driver fixes the ADR requires, installed once:
  - a hostname validator built on `cryptography` (DNS SANs only, a wildcard only as one whole left-most label, an IP only against IP SANs, no CN fallback, `\instance` stripped);

  - It refuses to patch a python-tds version whose layout it doesn't recognise.
- TLS is always on: a CA bundle is always passed (certifi, or a private CA written into a per-process 0700 directory), host validation is always on, and `sslmode` only accepts `verify-full`.
- ODBC lane: `driver: odbc` uses `mssql+pyodbc` with encryption forced on. DataQ never adds msodbcsql18 or pyodbc. If the lane is chosen but either is missing, Test Connection says so and explains how to build a derived image.
- Fabric on the default python-tds driver fails with a clear message: the known limitation plus the ODBC-lane fix, instead of the raw login error. The connection-test API now passes these DataQ-written messages through to the client, and only those.
- The shared base gained optional hooks rather than a fork. They are recorded as an ADR 0045 amendment:
  - `session_schema`: SQL Server can't scope a session to a schema, so the schema is handed to GX instead;
  - spec-level `destination_fields`;
  - `explain_failure`;
  - `unsupported_expectation_types`: the four regex checks have no T-SQL translation in GX and errored live, so they are refused at authoring time and hidden in the editor;
  - `llm_dialect`: the SQL generator's prompt names T-SQL.

| Persisted suite run | Pass, including Decimal failure samples written to JSONB |
| `#temp` tables | Need no extra grant for a `db_datareader` login |

It is named for the engine, not a cloud (ADR [0010](../adr/0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md)), and sits on the same generic SQL base as PostgreSQL. The driver decision and its trade-offs are [ADR 0044](../adr/0044-mssql-tds-driver-and-entra-auth.md). Live-verified against Azure SQL Database with both auth modes. - **Fields:** host (a bare hostname — e.g. `myserver.database.windows.net`; no scheme, port or `\instance`: connect to a named instance by its port), port (default 1433), database, an optional default schema (default `dbo`), and one of two **auth modes**: - **SQL login** — `user`, and the password as the secret. DataQ asks Entra ID for a token for `https://database.windows.net/` and presents it at login; the client secret never goes to the database server. Azure SQL, Synapse and Fabric. The principal must exist in the database (`CREATE USER [app-name] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER`) with read access. DataQ cannot read a client secret's expiry — track it in Entra ID and re-authenticate before it lapses. Managed identity and certificate credentials are not supported yet. - **TLS is always on and always verified.** There is no TLS mode to choose: every connection is encrypted, the server certificate must chain to a trusted CA (the public roots DataQ ships, or a **private CA certificate** you paste into the connection for a self-hosted server), and the hostname must match the certificate. Connecting by IP address fails for that reason — use the name on the certificate. The shipped driver speaks TLS 1.2; TDS 8 "strict" encryption is not supported yet. - **Read only — by grant, not by session.** Unlike PostgreSQL and MySQL, SQL Server has no per-session read-only switch, so DataQ **cannot make the server refuse a write**. The guards are the custom-SQL validator (which understands T-SQL `[bracket]` identifiers and refuses `OPENQUERY`/`OPENROWSET`/`OPENDATASOURCE`, `BULK`, `DBCC`, `WAITFOR`, `BACKUP`/`RESTORE` and the rest of the ADR 0019 list) and **the login you give DataQ, which must be read-only**: ```sql -- in the target database CREATE USER dataq_reader FOR LOGIN dataq_reader; -- or FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for Entra ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER dataq_reader; ``` Nothing else is needed: the session-scoped `#temp` tables some SQL Server queries use need no extra grant (verified with a `db_datareader`-only login). - **Two driver lanes** (`driver`): - **`python-tds`** (default) — pure-Python and MIT-licensed, shipped in the DataQ image. It covers SQL Server, Azure SQL and Synapse. - **`odbc`** — Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 through `pyodbc`. DataQ **does not ship** this driver (its licence does not allow us to redistribute it — ADR 0044), so this lane only works in an image **you** build on top of DataQ's — a sketch (DataQ's CI does not build or test it, since doing so would mean accepting the driver's licence): ```dockerfile FROM ghcr.io/theurgicduke771/dataq-backend:latest USER root RUN apt-get update && ACCEPT_EULA=Y apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ msodbcsql18 unixodbc && pip install pyodbc && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* USER 10001 ``` (add Microsoft's apt repository first, as Microsoft's install guide describes). Pick `odbc` on the connection; an optional `odbc_driver` names a different installed driver. If the lane is chosen but the driver or `pyodbc` is missing, **Test** says exactly that and how to fix it. On this lane the driver's own certificate checking applies (encryption required, server certificate verified against the image's trust store). - **Microsoft Fabric SQL endpoints need the ODBC lane today.** Over the default `python-tds` driver, Fabric rejects the login after routing it (a known incompatibility in that driver, still being worked on); Test and runs say so and point at the ODBC lane instead of showing the raw driver error. Fabric accepts Entra ID only, and two things are set up on the Fabric side: the tenant setting **Service principals can use Fabric APIs**, and a workspace role (or item permission) for the principal. If Fabric refuses the principal's login on the ODBC lane, Test names those two prerequisites. - **Everything runs in the database**, as on PostgreSQL. A run target takes no sampling block (so no `TABLESAMPLE`). Freshness reads `datetimeoffset` as the instant it is (offset honoured), `datetime2`/`datetime` as UTC, and `date` as midnight UTC. - **Regular expressions are not available**: T-SQL has no regex operator Great Expectations can translate to, so the four regex expectations are refused when you save them (and hidden in the editor). Use a custom-SQL check with `LIKE` or `PATINDEX`. Value-length checks use T-SQL `LEN`, which ignores trailing spaces. - **Type checks** (`to_be_of_type`, `in_type_list`) compare the bare type name: `DECIMAL` for `decimal(12,2)`, `INTEGER` for `int`, `NVARCHAR`, `DATETIME2`, `DATETIMEOFFSET`, `BIT`. - **The profiler** reports min/max as unavailable (null) for types SQL Server has no MIN/MAX for — `bit`, `xml`, `geography`/`geometry`, `text`/`ntext`/`image`, `json`, `vector` — and distinct count / top values as unavailable for all of those except `bit`.

=== docs/site/reference/feature-matrix.md #1
--- ours
ᵗ **SQL Server** — SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Synapse and (through the optional,
user-installed ODBC lane) Microsoft Fabric SQL endpoints; SQL login or Entra service principal;
TLS always verified; everything by pushdown. Unlike PostgreSQL and MySQL, sessions are **not**
read-only at the server (TDS has no such setting) — the login must be a `db_datareader`. Every
ticked row was verified by an **executed** run against a live Azure SQL database with both auth
modes (every SQL-capable expectation type, custom SQL, freshness over
`datetimeoffset`/`datetime2`/`date`, volume, anomaly measurement, profiler, schema drift,
comparison reads, inventory enumeration, browsing and a persisted suite run). That battery is
an opt-in live lane (`tests/integration/test_mssql_live.py`), not CI — no SQL Server can run in
CI without a commercial licence. The four regex expectations are refused on SQL Server (no T-SQL
translation in GX), and Fabric SQL endpoints do not work on the default driver yet — see
[Datasources & checks](../guides/datasources-checks.md#sql-server-azure-sql-fabric-t-sql).

||||||| 730fc215
--- theirs
ᵗ **Trino** — any cluster (incl. Starburst), one catalog per connection, and every store that
catalog federates; everything runs by pushdown on the cluster. The same battery was
**executed** against Trino 483 (the `memory` connector, and a mixed-case PostgreSQL table
through the `postgresql` connector), plus HTTPS with a private CA, password and JWT
authentication and file-based access control. Two engine facts: Trino has **no read-only
session**, so the read-only guarantee is the Trino user's own access control; and every name is
**lower case** — see [Datasources & checks](../guides/datasources-checks.md#trino).

for db, table in (("dataq_wh", "dbo.Orders"), ("dataq_lh", "dbo.orders")):
    cfg = spec.validate_config(
        {
            "host": FABRIC,
            "database": db,
            "auth_type": "entra_service_principal",
            "tenant_id": os.environ["ARM_TENANT_ID"],
            "client_id": os.environ["ARM_CLIENT_ID"],
            "driver": "odbc",
        }

        r = c.execute(text(f"SELECT * FROM {table}"))  # noqa: S608
        print(list(r.keys()))
        for row in r:
            print(tuple(row))
        print(c.execute(text(
            "SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME, TABLE_TYPE FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES"
        )).all())
        print(c.execute(text(
            "SELECT c.name, TYPE_NAME(c.user_type_id) FROM sys.columns c WHERE c.object_id = OBJECT_ID(:t)"
        ), {"t": table}).all())
        try:
            print("tablesample", c.execute(text(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {table} TABLESAMPLE (50 PERCENT)")).scalar())  # noqa: S608
        except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
            print("tablesample ERR", str(e)[:150])
    eng.dispose()
