**Two scoping rules had to reach the docstrings, not just the code.** The asset rollup is **workspace-true** (ADR 0037) — `list_visible_assets` takes no user and aggregates over ALL composing suites — so a model handed the number with no caveat will describe it as covering what the caller can see; `get_asset` therefore reports `restricted_suite_count` beside the grant-filtered suite list. Incidents, by the same ADR, stay **behind suite grants**: they are itemized failure evidence, not identity, so `get_incident` is 404-no-leak. That second rule is why **`incident:view` is a new gate value** rather than `suite:view` — the tool takes an *incident* id, so the sweep must materialise a real incident on the probe suite; a fabricated id raises "incident not found", which is in the accepted-denial vocabulary, and the sweep would pass **with the gate deleted**. The same vacuous-pass shape as `_REAL_RUN` / `_REAL_CHECK` / the 3A `CheckVersion` trap, hit for the fourth time. Both new gates were mutation-verified.

**The 404-no-leak rule moved out of the HTTP layer** into `incident_service.load_visible_incident`, shared by REST and MCP. A second hand-written copy of the only thing standing between an incident's evidence and an ungranted caller is the "guard at one door and not its sibling" shape, and that divergence is invisible until it leaks. Three honesty fields exist because the raw value is true and misleading alone — `monitored` (an unmonitored asset reads as a clean bill of health), `truncated` (against the real total; `len(page) == limit` is wrong on the exact-boundary page), and `lineage.qualified_by` (an empty graph behind a failing poller must never read as "nothing feeds this table" — #828). All four were exercised **through the real MCP protocol** against Postgres, with the boundary cases refused before the driver.

**Unplanned, user-directed, shipped 2026-08-16 — the ADR [0033](docs/site/adr/0033-workspace-roles-rbac.md) workspace-roles (RBAC) track, picked up from the `v1.1 Backlog`** (umbrella [#744](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/744), now closed): **five PRs** ([#1396](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1396)–[#1400](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1400)) taking all four slices plus the [#1118](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1118) class W5 had deferred *specifically* to this track. Authorization is now genuinely two axes: a stored **`users.role`** (`admin | member | viewer`) beside the per-suite `view/edit/admin/owner` ladder, both enforced on REST and MCP, both resolving **per request** — so a demotion lands on the target's next call, *including calls made with PATs they already hold*, with no token to revoke. `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` demotes to a **bootstrap seed + lockout break-glass** that only ever grants. **This closes gap G-e and the standing hole where any authenticated user — even one holding a single `view` share — could delete or re-credential the connection every suite in the workspace ran on** (⚠️ breaking for Members who managed connections; promote before upgrading, CHANGELOG carries the note). Roles are managed in **Admin → Members** behind a **last-admin guard that counts stored-role admins only** (an allowlist-resolved admin can vanish with the next deploy) under `FOR UPDATE`, with a structured audit line per change — the durable audit *table* stays ADR 0020's deferred #310.

**The reviews caught five things the design did not, and they share one shape — a rule that was stated but not enforced, or enforced in one place but not its sibling:** (1) a **third door** around the new gates — `POST /_probe/snowflake-suite` creates a Connection *and* a Suite and was ungated; the gates went on the resources' own routes and a sibling endpoint creating the same resources by another name was invisible to that reasoning; (2) the **last-admin guard was bypassable**, reading `previous` before taking the lock so a stale value skipped the check entirely and could leave *zero* admins; (3) **hiding a button is not gating a route** — a Member reaching `/connections/new` by bookmark or Back would have filled an entire credential form before learning it 403s; (4) the **Viewer edit-clamp was defeatable** by searching the directory again after selecting a viewer; (5) `*_secret_name` was **documented** as server-owned bookkeeping (`_carry_over_secret_name_keys` says so in as many words) and **enforced nowhere**, which made it a credential-exfiltration primitive. A comment is not a control. **[#1401](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1401) was filed as the one deliberately-left-open residual and then closed the same session by [#1403](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1403)** — #1400 closed the reference-*name* half, but the credential-bearing **URI** was still freely mutable, so an Admin could redirect a stored secret (with a `connection_versions` trail). Each adapter now declares `destination_fields` per credential slot and a config change that moves one is refused unless that credential is re-supplied: to send a credential somewhere new you must already know it. **And #1403's own review made the point a sixth time.** The guard shipped with `catalog_uri` under Iceberg's *catalog* slot only — true of a SQL catalog, and wrong for a REST one, where `catalog_properties` sends the PRIMARY secret (`secret_property: token`) as a bearer **to that same URI**. On the commonest REST shape — a `secret_ref` and no `catalog_secret_name` — the catalog slot found nothing stored and waved the move straight through. All seven regression tests reached `catalog_uri` through the catalog slot, so the hole was invisible to them by construction: **a test suite that only exercises one path through a rule cannot tell you the rule is incomplete.** The same review also found an empty-string secret satisfied "you re-supplied it" while blanking the credential — a pre-existing hole, since `reauth` had carried `min_length=1` since it shipped and create/update never did.

**The testing lesson repeated three times in one session and is now a standing rule: for a concurrency or ordering bug, writing the regression test is the easy half — proving it can FAIL is the half that matters.** Three separate tests here passed against the unfixed code and were caught only by mutation-checking them: a last-admin race driven sequentially (the interleaving never occurred), a Viewer-clamp test that skipped the "set `edit`" step (so there was nothing for the un-clamp to leak), and an OIDC role-forwarding test that never entered the branch it named. Two further habits earned their keep: **verify against the running artifact** — the per-role Playwright specs and the admin role-editor were validated in a real browser against CI's exact lane (a scratch dev-bypass API + its own Vite) after two rounds of CI-only locator failures, and the `users.role` migration was applied up *and* down against real Postgres on a populated table; and **check what the code does, not what the ticket says** — `docs/site/security/overview.md` already described this model (written ahead of the build) and was wrong in one place, claiming connection `test` was Admin-only when the ADR's normative matrix puts it at Member+.

## Appendix — Tech stack quick reference

| Layer | Tech |
|---|---|
| Backend framework | FastAPI (Python 3.13) |
| DQ engine | Great Expectations (GX Core) v1 — **pinned version** |
| Task queue | Celery + Redis |
| Database | PostgreSQL + Alembic |
| Frontend | React + Vite + Ant Design |
| SQL editor | Monaco |
| Auth | Three modes (ADR 0032): dev-bypass · email OTP (`dq_sess_` cookie sessions, local-stack default) · generic OIDC (`oidc-client-ts`, Azure AD + Cognito validated) + backend `fastapi-azure-auth`; PATs (`dq_live_`) for API/MCP |
| Authorization | **Two axes (ADR 0033):** stored workspace role `users.role` (`admin \| member \| viewer`) × per-suite grants (`view \| edit`, ADR 0027). Both enforced on REST and MCP; both resolved per request, so a role change applies to existing PATs immediately |
| Secrets | Azure Key Vault |
| Hosting | Azure Container Apps (API + worker + frontend; frontend = sole public surface, api internal — ADR 0028 §5) |
| Observability | Azure Application Insights + structlog |
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions |
| API docs | FastAPI Swagger + ReDoc |
| MCP | FastMCP (PrefectHQ) — 51 curated tools at `/mcp` (28 read-only, 18 that change state, 5 live-probe tools gated like writes; ADR 0008 + its #529 Tier-1/Tier-2 and #1424 Tier-3A/3B amendments + #1626's `get_doc` + #1775's channel read tools + #1710's `trace_column_lineage`) |
| Python tooling | conda + Black + Ruff + mypy + pytest + Bandit |
| Frontend tooling | Prettier + ESLint + Vitest + React Testing Library |
| Secret scanning | betterleaks (pre-commit + CI) |
| SAST | Bandit + CodeQL |

### Client-side MCP servers (`.mcp.json`)

Distinct from DataQ's **own** FastMCP server at `/mcp` (ADR 0008 — the 51 tools DataQ *serves* to AI clients), the repo-root **`.mcp.json`** configures MCP servers that AI assistants working in this repo *consume*:

| Server | Package (pinned major) | Publisher | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `context7` | `@upstash/context7-mcp@1` (npx) | Upstash | Up-to-date library docs lookup while coding |
| `azure` | `@azure/mcp@3.0.0-beta.29` (npx) — **exact**, see caveats | Microsoft (`github.com/microsoft/mcp`) | Container Apps / Key Vault / Monitor + App Insights KQL without hand-rolled `az rest` — the 2026-07-13 outage was invisible in `/healthz` and only the telemetry showed the exporter log loop |

- **Trust prompt:** Claude Code prompts once per machine before starting servers from a project `.mcp.json`; approve only if the list above matches what's in the file.
- **Pin majors, not `latest`** — same rationale as the GX pin.
- **Supply-chain cadence:** quarterly audit per CONTRIBUTING.md rule 39 (deprecated/yanked/publisher-transfer check before any bump).
- **`azure` caveats (deliberate, re-check before relying on it):** `@azure/mcp`'s only dist-tag is a **beta** (`3.0.0-beta.29`) — Microsoft-published, but pre-stable, so treat tool-surface changes as expected. **This is the one entry pinned to an exact version, not a major**, and deliberately so: npm excludes prereleases from a bare major range, so `@azure/mcp@3` resolves to *nothing* (`E404 No match found for version 3`) and the server would fail to launch. The "pin majors" rule assumes a package with a stable major; this one has none, so the version moves only on a conscious bump. It authenticates through the **local `az` CLI credential**, so it inherits whatever that identity can do — use it for reading state, and keep the Key Vault rule intact: **never surface or print a secret value**. Microsoft telemetry is disabled via `AZURE_MCP_COLLECT_TELEMETRY=false` in the server env. It is only useful while the Azure estate is up — drop the entry if the wind-down completes.

**Not added, and why** (so the decision isn't re-litigated): a **Postgres MCP** was evaluated for run/result triage and rejected on supply-chain grounds. The reference `@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres` is **deprecated**; the npm `postgres-mcp` is published by a single unaffiliated maintainer; the PyPI `postgres-mcp` declares **no license**, which CONTRIBUTING rule 40 / ADR 0031 forbids outright. `psql` over Bash already covers the need with zero added surface.

</system-reminder>

content.content:
the engine, not a cloud (ADR [0010](../adr/0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md)),
and sits on the same generic SQL base as PostgreSQL. The driver decision and its trade-offs are
[ADR 0044](../adr/0044-mssql-tds-driver-and-entra-auth.md). Live-verified against Azure SQL
Database with both auth modes.


      (add Microsoft's apt repository first, as Microsoft's install guide describes). Pick
      `odbc` on the connection; an optional `odbc_driver` names a different installed driver.
      If the lane is chosen but the driver or `pyodbc` is missing, **Test** says exactly that
      and how to fix it. On this lane the driver's own certificate checking applies (encryption
      required, server certificate verified against the image's trust store).
- **Microsoft Fabric SQL endpoints need the ODBC lane today.** Over the default `python-tds`
  driver, Fabric rejects the login after routing it (a known incompatibility in that driver,
  still being worked on); Test and runs say so and point at the ODBC lane instead of showing the
  raw driver error. Fabric accepts Entra ID only, and
  two things are set up on the Fabric side: the tenant setting **Service principals can use
  Fabric APIs**, and a workspace role (or item permission) for the principal. If Fabric refuses
  the principal's login on the ODBC lane, Test names those two prerequisites.
- **Everything runs in the database**, as on PostgreSQL. A run target takes no sampling block
  (so no `TABLESAMPLE`). Freshness reads `datetimeoffset` as the instant it is (offset
  honoured), `datetime2`/`datetime` as UTC, and `date` as midnight UTC.
- **Regular expressions are not available**: T-SQL has no regex operator Great Expectations can
  translate to, so the four regex expectations are refused when you save them (and hidden in
  the editor). Use a custom-SQL check with `LIKE` or `PATINDEX`. Value-length checks use
  samples, so this rarely matters, but every query is one network round trip — a suite run
  from a region far from the database is dominated by latency, not by the database.
- **Azure SQL serverless** databases pause when idle. The first login resumes them, which can
  take up to a minute: a run waits for it, a Test Connection gives up after 10 seconds — test
  again once the database is awake.

### Identifier casing (Snowflake / Unity Catalog / PostgreSQL)

content.content:
1	## Summary
2	
3	- **One `mssql` datasource type** for everything that speaks SQL Server's TDS protocol — SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Synapse, and Microsoft Fabric SQL endpoints — as a `SqlEngineSpec` on the generic SQL base (ADR 0045), per the accepted ADR 0044. Auth: `sql` (user + password) or `entra_service_principal` (tenant_id + client_id + client secret → `ClientSecretCredential` token for `https://database.windows.net/.default`, passed as `access_token_callable`; the secret never enters the URL).
4	- **Default driver `python-tds` + `sqlalchemy-pytds`** (both MIT, from installed metadata), with DataQ's own fixes in `datasources/mssql_tds.py`: a SAN hostname validator via `cryptography` (DNS SANs, single-label wildcard, IP only against IP SANs, no CN fallback, `\instance` stripped) replacing pytds's broken one, and named-instance routing (resolve only the host part). **TLS is always on**: a CA bundle (certifi, or the connection's private CA written into a per-process 0700 dir) is always passed and `validate_host` is always `True`; `sslmode` can only be `verify-full`.
5	- **Optional ODBC lane** (`driver: odbc` → `mssql+pyodbc`, Encrypt=yes, TrustServerCertificate=no, driver-native Entra). DataQ never adds msodbcsql18/pyodbc to requirements or images; if chosen but absent, Test Connection says exactly that and how to build a derived image. **Fabric on python-tds** (#2126) is reported honestly — the known limitation + the ODBC-lane fix — instead of the raw "system update" login error; on the ODBC lane an Entra login refusal names the Fabric prerequisites.
6	- **Generic base hooks** (no fork): `session_schema` (SQL Server can't scope a session to a schema → GX gets it), spec-level `destination_fields`, `credential_noun`, `explain_failure` (a DataQ-authored `SafeMonitorError` — the one failure text a connection test now returns to the client), `unsupported_expectation_types` (regex: no T-SQL translation in GX, refused at author time + hidden in the editor), `llm_dialect`. ADR 0045 amended.
7	- **Custom-SQL gate is now dialect-aware** (a real pre-existing gap, filed as #2134): lexes `[bracket]` / `` `backtick` `` identifiers per connection type (unknown dialect must pass every lexing), rejects nested block comments, ends `--` at a lone CR, and on mssql refuses `OPENQUERY/OPENROWSET/OPENDATASOURCE`, `BULK`, `DBCC`, `WAITFOR`, `BACKUP/RESTORE`, `WRITETEXT/UPDATETEXT`, `DENY`, `ENABLE/DISABLE`, … (T-SQL runs unseparated statements in one batch, and TDS has **no session read-only** — documented: the login must be `db_datareader`).
8	- Everything else via the shared registries: capability sets, inventory (`INFORMATION_SCHEMA` + `HAS_PERMS_BY_NAME`), browse, profiler column caps (live-verified T-SQL aggregate support), comparison reads (Core `.limit()` → `TOP`), auth markers (18456 with a 4060 veto; Entra secret markers shared with #2130), LLM dialect entry, migration widening the type CHECK (chained after MySQL's `d0cccce55833`), frontend form/targets/labels, docs.
9	
10	## Linked issue
11	
12	Fixes #1679. Fixes #2134. Refs #2126 (Fabric on python-tds). Filed from this work and left open: #2135, #2137, #2138.
13	
14	## Type of change
15	
16	- [x] feat — new functionality
17	- [x] fix — bug fix (custom-SQL lexer gap, #2134)
18	- [x] docs
19

PR #2139 (https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/2139) is at head `0032f325`: CI is fully green and the PR is **CLEAN / MERGEABLE**. I have not merged it. The PR body now says the live battery was re-run on the merged code, with the per-case results.

**Merge and migration**
- Merged origin/main, which now includes #2125 MySQL, #2130 OneLake and #2132 Trino. No force-push. All four engines are kept in every shared registry, type list, frontend list and doc.
- Trino already had its own versions of two things I had added, so I switched to its shapes rather than keep duplicates:
  - Trino made `destination_fields` a tuple on the engine spec, so mssql now uses the same shape.
  - Trino introduced a `textarea` field type, so I dropped my `multiline` type.
  - Trino calls its private-CA field `ca_bundle`, so I renamed mine from `ca_certificate` to match.
- Migration `0b451979c77d` now has `down_revision = 1a95d7c34808` (Trino). Its before/after type sets include `trino`: upgrade adds `mssql`, downgrade removes only `mssql`.
- `alembic heads` shows one head. On a fresh scratch DB it ran up (…→`d0cccce55833`→`1a95d7c34808`→`0b451979c77d`), then down, then up again, cleanly.
- My first up/down attempt reused an old scratch DB that had skipped Trino's migration. I dropped it and redid the run on a fresh one.

**Live runs on the merged code, python-tds lane**
- **17 passed**; the 2 Fabric-ODBC cases are skipped on this lane.
- Both auth modes pass: SQL login and service principal.
- Wrong password and wrong client secret (AADSTS7000215) are both classified as dead credentials.
- Connecting by IP is refused ("Certificate does not match host name"), and so is an untrusted CA ("certificate verify failed").
- Fabric on python-tds shows the honest limitation message, not the raw driver error.
- Every SQL-capable expectation type gives the expected verdict, in both auth modes.
- Freshness over datetimeoffset / datetime2 / date and volume both work. `datetimeoffset` honours its offset: `08:00-07:00` is read as 15:00 UTC.
- Anomaly measurement, the profiler, schema drift and comparison reads all pass.
- Inventory and browse offer only `dbo`.
- `execute_run` persisted results to a private Postgres app DB.

**Live runs, ODBC lane** (pyodbc on an isolated `PYTHONPATH` only for these runs, never in the shared env)
- Azure SQL, both auth modes: the full battery passed, 16/16. Connecting by IP is refused by the driver ("subject name does not match host name").
- **Fabric Warehouse `dataq_wh` and Lakehouse SQL endpoint `dataq_lh`** (service principal): Test Connection, checks including custom SQL, freshness and volume, the profiler, inventory (`<db>.dbo.<table>` only) and a persisted run all passed.
- The Fabric pair was last run separately, after the final timeout fix. The other runs finished before that change, and after it I only re-ran the unit tests, which passed.

**What the live runs found, and how each was handled**
- **Service-principal login on ODBC.** The driver's own `ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipal` login hung until `HYT00 Login timeout` on a wrong secret. Now DataQ mints the Entra token itself and passes it via `SQL_COPT_SS_ACCESS_TOKEN`, so a bad secret fails fast with AADSTS7000215.
- **FA005 with a token.** SQLAlchemy adds `Trusted_Connection=Yes` to a user-less pyodbc URL, and the driver refuses that next to a token. The URL is now a raw `odbc_connect` string.
- **Seven expectation types fail on Fabric** with error 15816, because GX builds `#temp` tables for them. They are the uniqueness, column-pair and multicolumn types. PR #2139 is at head `0032f325`, CI is fully green and GitHub shows it as clean and mergeable. I have not merged it. The PR description now says the live tests were re-run after the merge.

**Merge and migration**
- I merged main in without force-pushing; it now includes MySQL (#2125), OneLake (#2130) and Trino (#2132). All four SQL engines appear in every shared list, frontend list and doc.
- Where Trino had already added the same thing, I switched to Trino's version rather than keep two:
  - the destination-fields shape;
  - the textarea field type;
  - the field name `ca_bundle`.
- The SQL Server migration `0b451979c77d` now follows Trino's `1a95d7c34808`, so `alembic heads` shows one head.
- Its type list includes `trino`: upgrading adds `mssql` and downgrading removes only `mssql`.
- It ran up, down and up again cleanly on a fresh scratch database.

**Live tests on the merged code, default driver (python-tds)**: 17 passed. The 2 Fabric tests are skipped because they only run on the ODBC driver.
- Both login types work: SQL login and service principal. A wrong password and a wrong client secret are both reported as dead credentials.
- Connecting by IP is refused, and so is a certificate from an untrusted authority.
- Fabric on the default driver shows the clear "known limitation, use the ODBC lane" message.
- Every expectation type gives the expected result, freshness honours `datetimeoffset` offsets, and a full suite run saved its results end to end.

**Live tests, ODBC driver** (pyodbc was put on the path only for these runs, never in the shared environment)
- Azure SQL, both login types: all 16 pass.
- Fabric Warehouse and the Lakehouse SQL endpoint: connection test, checks, freshness, volume, profiler, inventory and a saved run all pass.
- The Fabric pair was last run separately, after the final timeout fix. The other ODBC runs finished just before that one-line change; only the unit tests were re-run after it.

**What the ODBC and Fabric runs found, all fixed in the PR**
- **Wrong client secret hung.** With the driver's own service-principal login, a bad secret waited for the full login timeout. DataQ now gets the Entra token itself, so a bad secret fails immediately with Entra's error.
- **Token rejected.** SQLAlchemy adds `Trusted_Connection=Yes` to a connection string with no user, and the driver refuses that next to a token. The connection string is now built by hand.
- **Seven check types fail on Fabric.** The uniqueness, column-pair and multi-column checks need a temporary table, which Fabric doesn't support (error 15816). Saving one on a Fabric connection is now refused, with a pointer to custom SQL.
- **Fabric system views** (`queryinsights`) appeared in inventory and browse; they are now hidden.
- **Slow first login.** A cold Lakehouse login exceeded the driver's default timeout, so runs on the ODBC driver now wait up to 60 seconds.

**Tests and checks**
- For 25 of the fixes, I broke the fix on purpose and confirmed its test then failed.
- Backend: 7232 tests passed, 97.23% coverage. Frontend: 1521 passed.
- Formatting, lint, type checks, the security scan, the dependency audit and the docs build are all clean.
- CodeQL raised two "unused global variable" comments, which kept the PR blocked. One was a false positive (the install guard flag, now a `threading.Event`) and one was a genuinely unused test marker, now removed. I resolved both threads.

**New follow-up issues** (milestone "v1.2 Backlog"):
- #2140: the check editor still lists the seven types that Fabric refuses; the error only appears on save.
- #2141: on the ODBC driver, closing already-closed connections logs ERROR lines. Results are not affected.
